knowledge_type_note: A board feature, mechanically countable, whose VALUE is conditional on being able to use it.

attributions.note: Treats space as one of the primary imbalances and stresses the entry-point requirement. Full text consulted.

history.notes: Space is standard vocabulary with no identifiable coiner; only its treatment as a named imbalance is attributable, and weakly.

engine_era_note: Engines carry space and mobility terms and value them, but considerably less than club instruction implies. They will concede space readily for concrete play, which is closer to the hypermodern position than the classical one.

preconditions: One side controls more squares behind its pawn front
indicators_for: The opponent's pieces have few squares and obstruct one another
An entry square exists or can be created
The extra space spans both wings, so the opponent cannot defend both
The opponent cannot trade pieces off
indicators_against: No entry point exists, so the territory buys nothing
The advanced pawns are fixed targets rather than a front
The cramped side can liquidate with exchanges
The space was gained by overextension the opponent can undermine
recognition.detector: pawnSpace + entrySquares in lib/features.js; the `space` matcher in lib/matchers.js
false_positive_traps: Counting controlled squares is mechanical and over-reports. Space with no entry point wins nothing.
Advanced pawns are not automatically a space advantage — they may simply be weak and fixed.
The cramped side's standard remedy is exchanging, so a space advantage that cannot prevent trades is temporary.

typical_plans: Avoid exchanges, improve pieces behind the front, then open a second front
Create an entry square before advancing further
As the cramped side: exchange pieces, and look for a freeing pawn break
typical_moves: A space-gaining pawn advance supported by pieces
A freeing break such as ...c5 or ...f6 by the cramped side
typical_pawn_structures: Maroczy Bind and similar space-clamping structures
strategic_consequences: Enables switching wings faster than the defender
Combines directly with the principle of two weaknesses, which needs exactly that ability

exceptions: Space with no way in is worth little.
Space bought by overextension is a liability — the hypermodern critique.
The cramped side exchanging pieces is the standard and effective antidote.
limitations: Countable but conditional: the count says nothing about usability.

TRAP 3 IS NOT IMPLEMENTED AND CANNOT BE, MECHANICALLY. 'The cramped side's standard remedy is exchanging, so a space advantage that cannot prevent trades is temporary' is a claim about what the position will BECOME, and no static feature answers it. The other two traps are built: an entry square is required (53.3% -> 34.6% of the 788 shipped positions), and a territory made entirely of weak, blocked pawns is refused (a further 1 position — it almost never binds, because a side with a real space advantage rarely has EVERY space-creating pawn weak, and the rate is recorded rather than talked up).

HUMAN-GROUNDED NEGATIVE ADDED 2026-09-02, and it is a live test of the entry-square guard rather than a vacuous one. Torre-Karpov, Bad Lauterberg 1977, move 26: White's pawns control NINE squares in Black's half against zero - as unambiguous a territorial advantage as this corpus contains, and six times the matcher's own threshold - and there is no entry square at all. Until this session the concept would have been reported here with confidence, in a position Stockfish scores at -3.01 after the move actually played. The annotators introduce the game as 'a great example of how not to play when you have space advantage'.
misconceptions: That more space is simply better. It is better if you can enter.
That advancing pawns gains space safely. It also fixes them and leaves holes behind them.

conflicts.resolution: The hypermodern position is precisely that space gained by pawn advance can be a liability, since the pawns become targets. Both are right conditionally: supported and expanded on time, space wins; static and overextended, it is a target. The deciding variable is whether the pawn front can be supported, not the amount of territory.

by_level.beginner: You control more squares, so your pieces have room and theirs are bumping into each other.
by_level.intermediate: A space advantage. Avoid trades, improve your pieces, and find the square you intend to invade on — space with no way in achieves nothing.
by_level.advanced: The value is the mobility difference and the ability to switch wings faster than the defender. Watch the cost: advanced pawns are fixed and leave holes.
by_level.master: Space combines directly with the two-weaknesses method, because that method needs exactly the ability to operate on both wings faster than the defence can follow.

by_depth.short: More room for your pieces, less for theirs.
by_depth.normal: A space advantage: you control more squares behind your pawn front. The value is mobility — their pieces get in each other's way. Avoid exchanges, and find an entry square, because space without a way in wins nothing.
by_depth.deep: Territory behind the pawn front, whose worth is the mobility difference rather than the squares themselves. Two corollaries matter more than the count: the cramped side should exchange pieces, since fewer pieces need fewer squares, and space must be usable — a big advantage almost certainly wins if a way can be found into enemy territory, which puts the emphasis on the entry point. The cost is real: advancing pawns fixes them and permanently uncovers the squares behind them, and space gained by overextension is a liability. That is exactly the hypermodern critique of the classical pawn centre.

explanations.lesson: Space is only worth what you can enter with. Before pushing another pawn, ask which square you intend to invade on.

definition_short: More squares controlled behind your own pawns, which gives your pieces room to manoeuvre and denies the opponent room to do the same.
definition_long:
Space is territory: the squares behind your pawn front, which your pieces can use and the opponent's cannot. Its value is not the territory itself but the MOBILITY difference — a cramped side's pieces get in each other's way and cannot be regrouped quickly, and the side with space can switch wings faster than the defender can follow.

Two standing corollaries follow, and both are more useful than the raw count. First, the cramped side should EXCHANGE PIECES: fewer pieces need fewer squares, and every trade relieves the cramp. Correspondingly, the side with space should avoid trades. Second, space must be USABLE — Silman's framing is that a big space advantage almost certainly wins if a way can be found to break into enemy territory, which puts the emphasis on the entry point rather than on the territory.

The cost side is real and easy to forget. Advancing pawns to gain space also fixes them, leaves squares behind them permanently uncovered, and can leave the advanced pawns as targets in an endgame. Space gained by overextension is a liability, which is precisely the hypermodern critique of the classical pawn centre.
